singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Affirming the consequent
If A then C; hence, A = C, but just because the consequent is true doesn't mean the antecedent must also be true.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Genetic fallacy
The genetic fallacy (also known as the fallacy of origins or fallacy of virtue) is a fallacy of irrelevance in which arguments or information are dismissed or validated based solely on their source of origin rather than their content.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Hasty generalization
Conclusion from sample too small or specialized to be representative

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Ad hominem 
("to the man") - attacks a person, rather than the argument

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Guilt by association
Discredit an argument shared by a socially demonized individual or social group

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Not a cause for a cause 
Assumes a cause for an event without evidence (confusing correlation with causation)

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Circular reasoning
(begging the question) one assumes the conclusion in one or more of the premises.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Slippery slope
Discredit position by arguing that acceptance will lead to undesirable sequence of events

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Composition and division
Fallacy of composition that bc the parts of a whole have a particular attribute, the whole must also have that attribute; fallacy of division infers that part of a whole must have some attribute bc that whole has that attribute.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
False dilemma 
A false dilemma is a fallacy that misrepresents an issue by presenting only two mutually exclusive options rather than the full, nuanced range of options. Here's a basic example: If we don't order pizza for dinner, we'll have to eat the week-old spaghetti in the fridge.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Straw man 
A straw man argument, sometimes called a straw person argument or spelled strawman argument, is the logical fallacy of distorting an opposing position into an extreme version of itself and then arguing against that extreme version.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Inductive argument 
If the premisses are true, then it is probable the conclusion will also be true (follows not with logical necessity, but probability).

singles.src: Kids in the House
singles.text: The executive branch, led by the President and the Vice President, enforces our laws. The judicial branch, led by the Supreme Court, interprets our laws. The legislative branch, which makes our laws, is the Congress.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Argument from consequences
The major fallacy of logos, arguing that something cannot be true because if it were the consequences or outcome would be unacceptable.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Equivocation 
The fallacy of equivocation occurs when a key term or phrase in an argument is used in an ambiguous way, with one meaning in one portion of the argument and then another meaning in another portion of the argument. Example: I have the right to watch "The Real World." Therefore it's right for me to watch the show.

singles.src: Gothic architecture: Can the 12th-century style radically change how we build today?
singles.text: For structural support, flying buttresses were used to give very tall columns additional support by, essentially, connecting them to more distant columns to lean against. The flying buttress defies gravity in appearing to leap from one column to another -- yet it carries significant weight, allowing the building to, paradoxically, appear more light, ethereal, and delicate.

singles.src: An Illustrated Book of Bad Arguments
singles.text:
Deductive argument 
If the premisses are true then the conclusion must be true (i.e., all men are mortal, Socrates is a man > Socrates must be mortal).

singles.src: The bewildering phenomenon of declining quality
singles.text: Artificial intelligence itself could deteriorate if no action is taken. In 2024, bot activity accounted for almost half of internet traffic. This poses a serious problem: language models are trained with data pulled from the web. When these models begin to be fed with information they themselves have generated, it leads to a so-called “model collapse.”

Concepts regarding the relationship of literature to social & cultural contexts in which they were produced.  4 concepts:
Metaphysical interprets work in continuity of historical process
Naturalistic/Positivistic sees work as sociological key to contemporary social meanings and values
Nationalistic sees work as expression of ideals shaped by national boundaries

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
Phenomenology
Existing only in the consciousness of the perceiver rather than a material state. Inspects without presuppositions about epistemology or ontology.

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
Absurdism (1942 - early 60s)
Human beings, cut off from their roots live in meaningless isolation in an alien universe. No way to establish significant relationship between human and  environment. Contains extreme forms of illogic, inconsistency and nightmarish fantasy.
Examples: Kafka's "Metamorphosis", Camus' "Myth of Sisyphus"

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
Existentialism
Concentrates on individual struggles with existence and society involving free will and sees inadequacy of human reason to explain universal philosophical questions.  Emphasizes that existence makes meaning out of nothingness.  Human beings have free will and are responsible for own choices in an absurd and meaningless world leading to anguish, loneliness, despair, nihilism and hopelessness.

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
Surrealism
Expression of imagination as realized in dreams and presented without conscious control. Typically juxtaposes incompatible concrete objects.
Examples: Nathanael West's "Dream Life of Balso Snell", Bob Dylan's "Tarantula"

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
Dadaism (1916 and 1924)
Ignored logical relationship between idea and statement and argued for absolute artistic freedom. Developed as protest against World War I. Replaced art and philosophy with conscious madness.

singles.src: Literary Studies of Critical Thought
singles.text:
New Humanism (1900–1940) 
Protest against modern philosophies and psychologies. Human will is free and sharp dualism between humans and nature.  Very brief movement.

Revival of Classicism after the Renaissance that countered Renaissance schools of thought with view that humankind is limited, dualistic and imperfect. Distrusted invention and innovation.
